name: Sir Richard Fanshawe
credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Richard Fanshawe was an English diplomat and royalist who served the Stuarts in Spain and Portugal. Gilfillan says he was born at Ware in 1607 or 1608 and was in Madrid in 1666.
He is best known as a translator, notably of Guarini's Il Pastor Fido (1647/48), and he published some original poems as well. Gilfillan prints his version of a Spanish sonnet, The Spring.

poems.title: The Spring, a Sonnet
poems.author: Sir Richard Fanshawe
poems.collection: Specimens with Memoirs of the Less-known British Poets, ed. George Gilfillan (1860)
poems.text:
Those whiter lilies which the early morn
Seems to have newly woven of sleaved silk,
To which, on banks of wealthy Tagus born,
Gold was their cradle, liquid pearl their milk.

These blushing roses, with whose virgin leaves
The wanton wind to sport himself presumes,
Whilst from their rifled wardrobe he receives
For his wings purple, for his breath perfumes.

Both those and these my Caelia's pretty foot
Trod up; but if she should her face display,
And fragrant breast, they'd dry again to the root,
As with the blasting of the mid-day's ray;
And this soft wind, which both perfumes and cools,
Pass like the unregarded breath of fools.

poems.title: A Rose
poems.author: Sir Richard Fanshawe
poems.collection: The Oxford Book of English Verse, 1250-1900, ed. A. T. Quiller-Couch (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1900)
poems.text:
Blown in the morning, thou shalt fade ere noon.
What boots a life which in such haste forsakes thee?
Thou’rt wondrous frolic, being to die so soon,
And passing proud a little colour makes thee.
If thee thy brittle beauty so deceives,
Know then the thing that swells thee is thy bane;
For the same beauty doth, in bloody leaves,
The sentence of thy early death contain.
Some clown’s coarse lungs will poison thy sweet flower,
If by the careless plough thou shalt be torn;
And many Herods lie in wait each hour
To murder thee as soon as thou art born--
  Nay, force thy bud to blow--their tyrant breath
  Anticipating life, to hasten death!
